title: Operation 'OPTical Illusion': How a Massive Fraud Probe Is Upending Indian Students' American Dreams
excerpt: A sweeping ICE investigation has exposed over 10,000 foreign students—many of them Indian—linked to phantom employers exploiting the OPT programme, sending shockwaves through the Indian diaspora's pipeline to the American workforce.
body:
For decades, the Optional Practical Training (OPT) programme has been the golden bridge between an American university degree and a career in the United States. For Indian students—who form the largest cohort of international graduates in STEM fields—OPT has been less a bureaucratic formality than a life plan. That plan is now under siege.

In what officials have dubbed Operation "OPTical Illusion," Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has uncovered a sprawling network of fraudulent employers that exploited the OPT system on an industrial scale. The probe has identified more than 10,000 foreign students, a significant proportion of them Indian nationals, who were linked to shell companies posing as legitimate employers. The operation has already yielded 15 arrests, with 11 of those detained being Indian citizens.

## Phantom offices, real consequences

The mechanics of the fraud were brazen. Investigators found companies with impressive-sounding names occupying empty offices—or no offices at all. These phantom employers generated fake human-resources documentation, fabricated payroll records, and issued fraudulent training plans to satisfy the requirements of OPT and STEM OPT extensions. Students received paperwork showing employment at technology or consulting firms that, upon inspection, had no clients, no revenue, and no actual operations.

ICE Acting Director Todd Lyons did not mince words. "OPT has become a magnet for fraud," he said, describing a system in which the gap between regulatory intent and on-the-ground reality had grown into a chasm. "We are seeing organised networks that treat immigration benefits as a commodity to be sold."

The consequences for students caught in the web are severe. Those found to have knowingly participated face visa cancellation, deportation, and potential bars on future re-entry to the United States. Even students who may have been unwitting participants—lured by recruiters promising easy employment authorisation—find themselves in legal jeopardy.

## A system under strain

The numbers tell a story of escalating enforcement. The United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) reported a 37 per cent increase in enforcement cases related to OPT fraud in 2026 compared with the previous year. The agency has deployed additional fraud-detection teams and is cross-referencing employer databases with tax filings and physical-address verification.

The crackdown comes amid a broader tightening of immigration enforcement under the current administration. Officials are reportedly considering several structural reforms: a temporary pause on visa processing for students at institutions with high fraud rates, the elimination of the "duration of status" designation that allows students to remain in the country as long as they maintain valid programme participation, and mandatory site visits to OPT employers.

## The diaspora ripple effect

For the Indian diaspora, the implications extend far beyond the individuals directly implicated. OPT and its STEM extension have been the primary mechanism through which Indian graduates transition from student visas to H-1B work permits—the well-worn path from campus to cubicle that has populated Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and research laboratories across the country.

Parents in Hyderabad, Pune, and Chennai who have invested lakhs in their children's American education are watching nervously. Immigration attorneys report a surge in consultations from Indian students seeking to verify the legitimacy of their OPT employers. Industry groups representing Indian IT professionals have urged USCIS to distinguish clearly between students who were complicit in fraud and those who were victims of sophisticated recruitment scams.

"The vast majority of Indian students on OPT are doing exactly what the programme intended—gaining practical experience at legitimate companies," said Aman Kapoor of Immigration Voice, an advocacy organisation. "But this scandal risks tarring an entire community."

## What lies ahead

Experts warn that the fallout may reshape the Indian student pipeline to the United States. Universities that have become dependent on international-student tuition—often heavily Indian—face reputational risk if their graduates are disproportionately linked to fraud networks. Some institutions have already begun issuing advisories urging students to conduct due diligence on prospective OPT employers.

For current OPT participants, the message from immigration authorities is unambiguous: verify your employer independently, ensure your work is genuine and matches your field of study, and retain documentation of actual work performed. In an era of heightened scrutiny, the burden of proof has shifted squarely onto the student.

The American dream, for Indian students at least, now comes with considerably more paperwork—and considerably more risk.
